readingSections.title: Process vs Thread (heavy vs light plus states)
readingSections.quickSummary: Process is a running program with its own address space, files, and one or more threads. Thread is the schedulable CPU within a process sharing the process memory. Create heavy for process, light for thread. Context switch on thread cheaper. States: new, ready, running, waiting/blocked, terminated; plus suspend variants.
content: A process is an instance of a program in execution. It owns an address space (code, data, heap, stack plus per-process metadata in the PCB — Process Control Block), a set of open files and sockets, and at least one thread. Processes are isolated — one cannot directly touch another's memory without OS help via shared memory or pipes. Creation via fork plus exec on Unix or CreateProcess on Windows is heavy and measured in microseconds to milliseconds.

A thread is the unit of CPU scheduling inside a process. All threads of a process share the same code, data, heap and files but each thread has its own program counter, register set and stack plus a Thread Control Block. Creating a thread is light — tens of microseconds — and switching between threads of the same process avoids swapping address spaces. The exam word task or lightweight process or LWP is a thread.

Concurrency vs parallelism: concurrent means interleaved on one core via context switches (not at the same instant but progression: one after another quickly). Parallel means truly simultaneous on many cores. A single-core machine can be concurrent but not parallel; a multi-core machine can be both. Multithreading exploits both when the OS schedules threads across cores.

Life cycle: new while being admitted, ready waiting for the CPU, running on the CPU, waiting or blocked until an event (I/O complete, lock), and terminated after exit. Preemptive kernels can move a running process to ready on a timer tick or arrival of a higher priority job; cooperative waits for voluntary yields. Diagram-wise the exam often draws the classic five-state model plus suspend ready and suspend waiting that swap a process to disk.

Small facts that reappear. User threads managed in user space by a thread library (e.g. green threads) vs kernel threads managed by the OS — many-to-one maps many user threads to one kernel thread (poor parallelism), one-to-one maps each user to a kernel thread (common, e.g. Linux NPTL), many-to-many mixes. The exam writes Java threads are user-level but the modern JVM maps each to a kernel thread — that mix is the mark.

subsections.title: PCB vs TCB contents in 15 seconds
subsections.content: PCB holds process-wide state: PID, parent, address space pointers, open file table, signal mask, scheduling priority, accounting, and list of threads. TCB holds per-thread state: thread ID, registers including PC and stack pointer, stack bounds, scheduling state, and blocked reason. Swap TCB on thread switch; swap PCB plus page tables on process switch.

subsections.title: Fork plus exec vs clone
subsections.content: fork duplicates the process (copy-on-write pages today), child gets a copy of the parent's address space and file descriptors. exec replaces the child image with a new program. Threads share via clone with shared address space flags. AXIS rarely asks to run fork but does label fork as heavy and thread creation as light.

quickRevision: Process running program with its own address space plus files plus one or more threads via heavy creation and PCB; thread schedulable CPU inside process sharing memory with its own stack plus registers and TCB.
Process isolated; thread shared memory of the process — thread creation and context cheaper.
States: new -> ready -> running -> waiting/blocked -> terminated; preemptive can preempt running to ready; plus suspend variants swapping to disk.
Concurrent interleaved on one core vs parallel truly simultaneous on many cores; multithreading uses both when OS spreads threads.
User vs kernel threads: many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many; modern JVM one-to-one is the AXIS expectation.
tricks: Any answer that says threads have separate address spaces like processes is wrong — threads of one process share the process address space.
Do not attach heavy creation to threads — fork plus exec is heavy; thread is light.
Ready vs running is CPU held vs waiting for CPU. Blocked vs ready after I/O is blocked waiting for event vs ready for CPU.
patterns: 'Running program with its own address space?' -> Process. 'Schedulable unit inside sharing memory?' -> Thread.
'Heavy create with PCB and copy?' -> Process via fork. 'Light create with TCB share?' -> Thread.
'Interleaved on one core vs simultaneous on many?' -> Concurrent vs parallel.
'Same process shared heap but own stack?' -> Thread. 'New->ready->running->waiting->terminated?' -> Process life cycle.

pyqPatterns.source: Gate / AXIS — process vs thread plus states plus PCB/TCB, every year
pyqPatterns.question: Differentiate process vs thread plus PCB vs TCB plus thread types plus map plus concurrent vs parallel plus life cycle diagram?
pyqPatterns.approach: Process heavy with address space and PCB; thread light schedulable with TCB shares process memory; concurrent vs parallel vs parallelism; five-state plus suspend.

pyqPatterns.question: Why is thread creation faster than process creation?
pyqPatterns.approach: No need to duplicate address space and files — share process memory plus heap plus files, only create stack plus registers.

readingSections.companyNote: 1-2 questions per paper on process vs thread plus states or PCB/TCB plus concurrent vs parallel.

readingSections.title: Scheduling: Preemptive vs Nonpreemptive plus FCFS/SJF/SRTF/RR/Priority plus Metrics
readingSections.quickSummary: Scheduler picks who runs. Metrics: CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround (finish minus arrival), waiting, response, fairness. FCFS nonpreemptive by arrival. SJF nonpreemptive shortest next optimal for average wait but needs burst estimate and starves long. SRTF preemptive SJF. Priority picks highest priority may starve. RR time-quantum round-robin fair for interactive.
content: Goals that decide trade-offs: maximize CPU utilization and throughput (jobs per unit time) while minimizing turnaround (arrival to finish, includes waiting plus running), waiting (in ready queue), response (arrival to first CPU for interactive), and variance fairness plus starvation. Real OSes balance many, not one. AXIS often lists these five metrics and asks which FCFS optimizes vs which RR optimizes.

FCFS (First-Come First-Served) runs in arrival order nonpreemptively. Simple and starvation-free but convoy effect kills average wait when a long job holds the head and many short arrive behind it. Turnaround equals waiting plus burst; waiting accumulates the convoy. The exam's FCFS with one long at front is the average-wait trap where SJF beats it badly.

SJF (Shortest Job First) picks the shortest burst among ready nonpreemptively and is provably optimal for minimum average waiting among nonpreemptive policies. SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First) is the preemptive twin — if a new shorter job arrives while one runs, it preempts. Both need burst estimates which are imperfect and both starve long jobs without aging. Priority scheduling picks highest priority (externally ranked) nonpreemptively; preemptive priority preempts on higher arrival plus aging slowly raises waiting priority to combat starvation.

Round-Robin (RR) gives each ready process a time quantum Q and cycles. Small Q favors response and fairness but causes many context switches and cache disruption; large Q approaches FCFS. Waiting in RR includes many small slices, not one long head wait. The exam writes Q = 2 vs Q = 4 and asks for Gantt vs averages — quantum size moves boundaries tick by tick.

Multilevel queues and feedback: the OS often mixes policies — foreground interactive RR-like while background batch FCFS-like, with feedback that demotes misbehaving jobs to lower queues. The exam rarely asks to run feedback beyond the name, but it recognizes multilevel as the diagram that separates foreground vs background.

subsections.title: Gantt computation that saves marks
subsections.content: Draw one row per CPU and fill bursts in policy order including preemptions at each arrival tick. For each process record arrival, start, finish. Turnaround = finish - arrival. Waiting = turnaround - burst. Response = first start - arrival. Average each over jobs. With RR also record slice per quantum.

subsections.title: Optimality claim that AXIS loves
subsections.content: Shortest next is optimal for minimum average waiting among nonpreemptive choices. Any paper that asks proven optimal for that metric expects SJF/SRTF by name. No other nonpreemptive beats SJF in that metric if bursts are known.

quickRevision: Metrics: utilization plus throughput high vs turnaround plus waiting plus response plus fairness low.
FCFS nonpreemptive by arrival: simple starvation-free but convoy bad average wait with one long at head.
SJF nonpreemptive shortest next optimal for average wait; SRTF preemptive twin; both starve long without aging and need estimates.
Priority picks highest priority via ranking, needs aging against starvation; preemptive priority preempts on higher arrival.
RR time-quantum round-robin fair for interactive; small Q good response many switches, large Q towards FCFS; multilevel queues split foreground vs background.
tricks: Any answer that says FCFS is optimal for average waiting is wrong — SJF holds that crown among nonpreemptive.
Do not confuse SRTF vs SJF: same shortest rule, SRTF preemptive and SJF not — arrival during execution matters only for SRTF.
Aging fixes priority starvation but not FCFS convoy — aging raises priority, convoy is ordered by arrival not priority.
patterns: 'One long at head many shorts behind?' -> Convoy under FCFS; SJF wins.
'Proven optimal for average waiting nonpreemptive?' -> SJF (preemptive twin is SRTF).
'Preempt on higher arrival plus anti-starvation?' -> Priority plus aging.
'Time-quantum fair for interactive?' -> Round-Robin; small Q good response, large Q towards FCFS.
'Mixed foreground vs background?' -> Multilevel plus feedback.

pyqPatterns.source: Every AXIS paper — scheduling plus metrics plus Gantt, guaranteed
pyqPatterns.question: FCFS vs SJF vs SRTF vs RR vs Priority plus averages plus convoy plus aging?
pyqPatterns.approach: FCFS arrival order, SJF shortest nonpreemptive optimal, SRTF preemptive twin, RR quantum with Gantt tick, Priority with aging.

pyqPatterns.question: Given bursts plus arrivals plus quantum Q plus priorities, compute average turnaround vs waiting or which starves?

readingSections.title: Deadlocks: Four Conditions, Graph, Prevention vs Avoidance vs Detection vs Recovery plus Dining
readingSections.quickSummary: Deadlock is a cycle of waits. Necessary four: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait (all four for deadlock, but four together do not guarantee). Handle by prevention (break one), avoidance via Banker's safe check, detection plus recovery, or ignore (ostrich). Dining philosophers is the canonical starvation plus deadlock case.
content: Deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another in the set, so none can proceed. The four necessary conditions: mutual exclusion (resource held by one at a time), hold and wait (holder waits for another while keeping its own), no preemption (cannot forcibly take the held resource), and circular wait (chain that circles: P1 waits for P2 while P2 waits for P1 or longer cycle P1->P2->P3->P1). All four must hold for deadlock, but four together do not guarantee deadlock on every path — they are necessary not sufficient for a cycle to be realized.

Graph view: resource allocation graph with process nodes and resource instances plus request edges and assignment edges. A cycle in the graph indicates deadlock when each resource in the cycle has a single instance; with multiple instances a cycle is a warning not a proof. AXIS commonly draws the classic two-process two-resource cycle R1 held by P1 wanted by P2 and R2 held by P2 wanted by P1.

Handling strategies. Prevention breaks one of the four: break mutual exclusion via sharable resources where possible, break hold-and-wait via all-or-nothing request (request all at once), break no-preemption via allow preemption on wait, break circular wait via total order on resources (always request in numeric order). Avoidance does not break statically but checks safety before granting — Banker's algorithm checks whether the system stays in a safe state (a sequence that can run to completion) and denies the request if it would make it unsafe. Detection lets deadlocks happen and runs a cycle detector periodically plus recovery by aborting or preempting until the cycle breaks. Ignorance (ostrich) lets deadlocks be rare versus recovery cost — many general-purpose OSes take this and expect the operator.

Banker's algorithm at intuition level: each process declares its maximum need per resource type upfront. System tracks allocated plus available. Before granting a request it simulates the grant and tests existence of a safe sequence where every remaining process can complete with hypothetical future allocations under its max. If none exists the state is unsafe and the request waits. AXIS asks whether immediate granting keeps the state safe — compute safe sequence or not.

Dining philosophers frames starvation plus deadlock: N philosophers at a round table with N forks, each needs two forks to eat and thinks otherwise. Classical deadlock when each grabs left and waits for right. Prevention via global fork ordering or limit of N-1 eaters or asymmetry prevents circular wait. Classic exam story: 5 philosophers, 5 forks, each picks left first -> deadlock. Change order for one to pick right first -> deadlock-free.

subsections.title: Prevention vs avoidance vs detection in one sentence each
subsections.content: Prevention breaks one condition statically before allocation. Avoidance checks dynamic safety before granting. Detection allows then finds cycles plus recovers. Ostrich ignores because deadlocks are rare for the cost.

subsections.title: Safe vs unsafe is not deadlocked vs not
subsections.content: Safe means a sequence exists to finish every process even under max needs. Unsafe means no such sequence — deadlock may occur if worst-case requests arrive, but not necessarily right now. Avoidance denies requests that would make the state unsafe, not only those that are immediately deadlocked.

quickRevision: Deadlock is wait cycle plus four necessary: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Prevention breaks one: no hold-and-wait or ordered requests etc. Avoidance Banker's safe check before grant. Detection cycle plus abort/preempt. Ostrich ignore.
Resource graph cycle means deadlock when single instance per type; multi-instance cycle is warning not proof.
Banker declares max per type plus tracks allocated plus available; grants only safe states where a completion sequence exists.
Dining philosophers 5 pick-left deadlock vs alternate ordering or N-1 limit prevents circular wait.
tricks: Any answer that says three of the four can still deadlock is wrong — all four must hold for deadlock.
Do not equate unsafe with deadlocked — unsafe may still run but could deadlock under max; avoidance denies unsafe, not only deadlocked.
Graph cycle alone is insufficient with many instances per resource — need resource instance count.
patterns: 'Four necessary for deadlock?' -> Mutual exclusion plus hold and wait plus no preemption plus circular wait.
'Check before granting?' -> Banker's avoidance via safe sequence.
'Break one condition statically?' -> Prevention (hold-and-wait or circular wait via ordering).
'Detect plus abort after?' -> Detection plus recovery.
'5 philosophers each left then right?' -> Deadlock via circular wait; ordering fix breaks it.

pyqPatterns.source: Every AXIS paper — deadlock plus Banker, guaranteed
pyqPatterns.question: Which condition or which handling fixes it or is this state safe via Banker's or which philosophers fix works?
pyqPatterns.approach: Four plus break-one is prevention, Banker safe if a completion sequence exists, diamond vs chain plus N-1 for dining.

pyqPatterns.source: Gate / placement — graph cycle vs instances
pyqPatterns.question: Does this allocation graph imply deadlock with many instances?
pyqPatterns.approach: Single type cycle implies deadlock; multi-instance cycle warning not proof.

readingSections.companyNote: Deadlock plus Banker's safe plus dining prevention appears as a 2-item set.

readingSections.title: Memory Management: Contiguous vs Paging vs Segmentation plus Replacement
readingSections.quickSummary: Memory is scarce and fragmented. Contiguous needs one block and fragments externally; paging splits into equal frames and pages plus TLB plus replacement (FIFO/LRU/Optimal/Clock); segmentation splits by logical chunks with sharing. Virtual memory plus demand paging loads pages on fault; thrashing is excess paging; copy-on-write shares then splits.
content: Contiguous allocation places each process in one continuous block. First-fit picks the first hole that fits, best-fit the smallest fitting, worst-fit the largest. External fragmentation leaves many small holes none big enough; compaction defragments by moving blocks but is expensive. Internal fragmentation is waste inside an allocated block or page/segment due to rounding up.

Paging solves external fragmentation by splitting physical memory into equal frames and virtual memory into equal pages, with a page table mapping virtual page number to frame plus offset. The TLB caches recent translations; a TLB hit avoids a page table walk. Caching TLB is like DNS cache but for addresses. Demand paging loads a page only on a page fault (trap when needed) plus replacement picks a victim when no free frame exists.

Replacement policies decide the victim. FIFO evicts the oldest loaded (simple but Belady anomaly can occur where more frames increase faults). LRU evicts the least recently used (good locality, needs tracking, stack-friendly). Optimal (OPT or Belady ideal) evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future (unreal but the lower bound against which LRU is measured). Clock (second-chance) approximates LRU with one reference bit plus a circular hand. The exam draws the reference string and asks for fault count per policy — fault count is the metric of choice.

Segmentation splits by logical units (code, data, stack) that are variable sized and sharable: libraries map the same segment into many address spaces, which paging alone can simulate with shared frames but segmentation supports naturally. Paged segmentation (segment plus pages) and huge pages plus TLB size vs page fragmentation trade off. Pages fix external fragmentation but have internal waste per page (average half a page per segment).

Virtual memory plus thrashing: when the working set does not fit, the OS faults constantly while making no forward progress — thrashing. Fixes: swap more jobs out, buy frames, or use working-set or Page-Fault-Frequency based admission. Copy-on-write after fork plus shared libraries are features that avoid copying bytes until writes diverge.

subsections.title: Fault count comparison in one glance
subsections.content: FIFO is oldest. LRU is least recently used. Optimal is farthest future. Clock is hand with reference bits approximating LRU. For the canonical string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4 plus 3 frames, faults are FIFO 7, LRU 6, Optimal 5 — that hierarchy holds for that string and often resembles real ordering even if not universal.

subsections.title: External vs internal in 10 seconds
subsections.content: External many small holes between blocks — compaction fixes but paging removes the need. Internal waste inside the last page or segment due to rounding even though external has gone. AXIS often writes many small holes vs waste inside a page and expects external vs internal respectively.

quickRevision: Contiguous one block: first/best/worst fit plus external many small holes fixed by compaction, internal waste inside block.
Paging frames equals pages, page table via VPN to frame plus offset, TLB caches translations, demand paging on fault.
Victim policies: FIFO oldest (Belady), LRU least recent, Optimal farthest ideal, Clock hand second-chance.
Segmentation logical variable chunks sharable; paged helps both benefits; internal half-page average still.
Virtual memory thrashes when working set overcommits — fix swap out or add frames; copy-on-write shares then splits after fork.
tricks: Any answer that says Belady can happen under LRU is wrong — Belady disproves stack property; LRU is stack and thus Belady-free, FIFO is not.
Do not attach trunk to external fragmentation still present under paging — paging removes external, keeps internal.
Demand paging on TLB hit does not fault — hit avoids table walk, misses need table then perhaps fault.
patterns: 'One block per process many holes?' -> Contiguous external. 'Waste inside page?' -> Internal.
'VPN to frame plus offset via table plus TLB plus fault?' -> Paging.
'Oldest vs least recent vs farthest future?' -> FIFO vs LRU vs Optimal.
'Logical variable sharable chunks?' -> Segmentation.
'Fits never exceeds frames -> thrashing?' -> Page-fault storm.

pyqPatterns.approach: Simulate: FIFO queue age, LRU stack recency, Optimal scan future, Clock hand bits approximation.

readingSections.title: Exam OS Synthesis: process vs scheduling vs deadlock vs memory plus IPC
readingSections.quickSummary: Life cycle decides heavy vs light plus states; scheduling picks policy plus metrics plus starvation; deadlock four plus handling via prevention vs avoidance vs detection; memory paging vs segmentation plus victim faults; IPC and sync via pipes plus shared memory plus mutex plus semaphore plus monitor stitch them.
content: State plus creation row: new->ready->running->waiting->terminated, suspend variants; process heavy fork vs thread light; user vs kernel thread many-to-one vs one-to-one; PCB vs TCB contents; concurrent vs parallel. The exam often mixes this with memory — do not let the mix distract from the heavy vs light split.

Scheduling row: FCFS arrival order nonpreemptive with convoy, SJF shortest nonpreemptive optimal for average wait, SRTF preemptive twin, Priority via ranking plus aging, RR quantum for interactive, multilevel foreground vs background. Metrics turnaround minus arrival, waiting minus burst, response first start minus arrival, plus utilization plus throughput plus fairness. Gantt ticking is the calculation skill.

Deadlock plus sync row: four necessary plus prevention break-one vs avoidance Banker's safe vs detection cycle vs ostrich; allocation graph cycle plus single-instance proof; dining philosophers circular wait fix via ordering or N-1; synchronization of access to shared data uses locks: mutex for critical section, semaphore for counting, monitor plus condition for encapsulated wait, spin versus sleep trade-offs.

Memory row: contiguous first/best/worst plus external vs compaction; paging fixed split plus TLB plus fault plus replacement FIFO/LRU/Optimal/Clock; segmentation variable sharable; virtual plus thrashing via working set; copy-on-write. The exam loves Belady as the gotcha that only FIFO among the trio exhibits.

IPC stitching: pipes anonymous plus named FIFO for streaming bytes between processes plus message queues plus shared memory for bulk via mapping plus signals. Threads of one process communicate via shared memory with synchronization instead. AXIS writes IPC type questions as pipes vs shared memory — streaming vs shared mapping is the discriminant.

subsections.title: One-pass elimination for mixed OS items
subsections.content: Item lists four statements mixing PCB vs scheduling vs deadlock vs paging. If the stem says drop vs alert, ignore for OS scheduling but check active vs passive vocabulary does not leak from networking — keep OS row: hold-and-wait vs hold plus wait naming is exact, polling vs quantum vs sharing belongs to scheduling, not security.

subsections.title: When both isolation plus scheduling matter together
subsections.content: A pipeline of parallel threads on a multi-core guest VM scheduled both by the guest kernel and the host hypervisor is two-level scheduling. Guest chooses which thread of its process runs, host chooses which vCPU of which VM runs. Layering doubles but each layer still uses FCFS vs SJF vs RR style policies.

quickRevision: Heavy fork plus exec plus PCB vs light thread plus TCB plus sharing; five-state plus suspend; user vs kernel many-to-one vs one-to-one; concurrent vs parallel.
FCFS arrival, SJF shortest nonpreemptive optimal, SRTF preemptive twin, Priority ranking plus aging, RR quantum with Gantt tick, turnaround minus arrival etc.
Deadlock four plus handling break-one vs Banker safe vs detection plus graph cycle, dining N-1 or ordering fixes.
Memory contiguous vs paging frames plus TLB plus faults FIFO/LRU/Optimal/Clock vs segmentation vs virtual thrashing plus copy-on-write plus internal vs external fragmentation.
IPC pipes vs shared memory vs signals plus sync via mutex vs semaphore vs monitor.
tricks: Any answer that mixes hold and wait wording is sensitive — hold and wait is one of the four: keeping one while requesting another.
Do not attach Belady to LRU — LRU is stack and thus Belady-free; only FIFO among FIFO/LRU/Optimal invites Belady.
External fragmentation is not a paging problem — paging removes external; contiguity removal is the paging win.
patterns: 'Heavy with own address space vs light sharing?' -> Process vs thread.
'FCFS vs SJF vs Priority vs RR?' -> Arrival order vs shortest optimal vs ranking plus aging vs quantum.
'Four for deadlock plus handling?' -> Four necessary plus break-one vs Banker vs detection plus dining N-1 or ordering.
'Oldest vs least recent vs farthest?' -> FIFO vs LRU vs Optimal.
'Streaming bytes between processes?' -> Pipe vs shared memory mapping.

pyqPatterns.approach: One pass: heavy vs light plus states for process; arrival vs shortest vs ranking plus aging vs quantum for scheduling; four plus handling for deadlock; paging vs segment plus victim faults for memory plus pipes vs shm for IPC.

formulas.title: Process vs Thread split with States and PCB vs TCB

formula.latex: Process=program+addr\;space+files+threads\;heavy\;PCB \;|\; Thread=sched\;inside\;sharing+stack\;TCB \;|\; new\to ready\to running\to waiting\to term
formula.text: Process program+addr space+files+threads heavy PCB | Thread sched inside sharing+stack TCB | new to ready to running to waiting to term

formulas.whenToUse: Any process vs thread vs PCB vs state vs concurrent vs user vs kernel MCQ.
explanation: Process is a running program with its own virtual address space plus files plus one or more threads via heavy fork plus exec, tracked in a PCB.
Thread is the CPU-schedulable unit inside a process sharing code plus data plus heap plus files, with own PC plus stack plus registers in a TCB.
States: new pending admission, ready waiting for CPU, running on CPU, waiting/blocked awaiting I/O or lock, terminated done, plus suspend ready/waiting swapped to disk.
Concurrent interleaved on one core vs parallel simultaneous on many; threads exploit both when OS spreads them.
User threads many-to-one via library vs kernel one-to-one via OS vs many-to-many mix; modern JVM one-to-one is AXIS expectation.

example.prompt: Thread vs process memory and creation: which shares which and which is faster to create?
steps: Threads of one process share its heap plus code plus data plus files; only stacks plus registers are separate.
Process creation duplicates address space and file table via fork plus exec; thread only needs stack plus TCB.
Thread creation is lighter and faster than process creation.
example.answer: Threads share process heap/code/data/files plus own stack; process heavy vs thread light

formulas.memoryTip: Heavy House Process with Land, Light Thread lives inside. PCB Pink Card for Process, TCB Tiny Card for Thread. New Ready Runners Wait Terminate.
formulas.commonMistake: Threads have separate address spaces — they share the process address space; processes are the isolated units.

formulas.title: Scheduling Policies and Metrics

formula.text: FCFS arrival | SJF shortest nonpreempt opt | SRTF preempt shortest | Priority rank+aging | RR quantum | Turnaround finish-arrival Waiting turnaround-burst

formulas.whenToUse: Any FCFS vs SJF vs SRTF vs Priority vs RR vs convoy vs aging vs Gantt average MCQ.
explanation: FCFS arrival order nonpreemptive simple starvation-free with convoy bad average waiting when one long at head.

SJF shortest among ready nonpreemptive is provably optimal for minimum average waiting; SRTF is its preemptive twin that preempts on shorter arrival; both need estimates and starve long without aging.
Priority picks highest priority via ranking, needs aging to raise waiting priority and avoid starvation; preemptive priority preempts on higher arrival.
Round-Robin time quantum cycles, small Q favours response and fairness but many switches, large Q approaches FCFS; multilevel splits foreground vs background with feedback.
Metrics: turnaround = finish - arrival, waiting = turnaround - burst, response = first start - arrival; Gantt plus those averages is the calculation skill.

example.prompt: Three jobs bursts 8, 4, 2 arrive together at 0. Average waiting under FCFS order 8 then 4 then 2 vs SJF order 2 then 4 then 8?
steps: FCFS Gantt: 0-8 first, 8-12 second, 12-14 third; waits are 0, 8, 12 so average (0+8+12)/3 = 6.66.
SJF order 2 then 4 then 8: Gantt 0-2, 2-6, 6-14; waits 0, 2, 6 average (0+2+6)/3 = 2.66.
SJF lower average waiting — optimality among nonpreemptive.
example.answer: FCFS average ~6.7, SJF average ~2.7, SJF better (optimal) under same set

formulas.memoryTip: FCFS First, SJF Shortest, SRTF Remains shortest, Priority ranked plus Aging, Round-Robin Repeats with Quantum. SJF is Star for minimum average wait.
formulas.commonMistake: FCFS optimal for average waiting — SJF holds that crown among nonpreemptive.

formulas.title: Deadlock Four plus Graph plus Handling

formula.text: Four ME HoldWait NoPrempt CircWait | Prevention break one | Avoidance Banker safe | Detection cycle | Dining N-1 or ordering

formulas.whenToUse: Any deadlock condition or graph or prevention vs avoidance vs detection or dining MCQ.
explanation: Deadlock is wait cycle plus four necessary: mutual exclusion holder one at a time, hold and wait keeps own waits for another, no preemption cannot forcibly take, circular wait chains and circles.
Prevention breaks one statically: no hold-and-wait via all-or-nothing, preemption allowed, circular wait via total order on resources.
Avoidance via Banker's declares max per type plus available, grants only if a safe completion sequence exists after grant; unsafe denied not yet deadlocked.
Resource graph cycle indicates deadlock when single instance per resource type; multi-instance cycle warning not proof.
Dining philosophers N pick left deadlock; break circular by global ordering or limit to N-1 eaters or asymmetry.

example.prompt: Two processes each hold one resource and want the other's — which deadlock condition and fix handles this?
steps: Holds one waits for other is hold and wait plus mutual exclusion plus no preemption plus circle P1->P2->P1.
All four necessary are present and graph has a cycle so deadlock with single instances.
Break circular via ordered requests or allow preemption, or use avoidance Banker to deny the second wait.
example.answer: Hold and wait plus circular wait; break by ordering or preemption or Banker avoidance

formulas.memoryTip: ME Hold NoPre Circ is four. Prevention Prevents broken one, Avoidance Asks Banker safe, Detection Finds cycle, Dining Dines with ordering.
formulas.commonMistake: Unsafe already deadlocked — unsafe may still run but could deadlock under worst-case max; avoidance denies unsafe, not only deadlocked.

formulas.title: Memory: Contiguous vs Paging vs Segmentation plus Replacement

formula.text: Contig one block extern vs internal | Paging frames+pages+TLB+fault | FIFO/LRU/Opt/Clock | Seg logical sharable

Paging splits physical into frames and virtual into pages, page table via VPN to frame plus offset, TLB caches translations, demand paging faults on need, replacement picks victim.
FIFO oldest, LRU least recent (stack, Belady-free), Optimal farthest future ideal, Clock hand second-chance approximation.
Segmentation logical variable sharable plus paged segmentation combines both plus huge pages vs TLB vs internal trade.

example.prompt: Reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4 with 3 frames faults under FIFO vs LRU vs Optimal?
steps: FIFO oldest queue age simulation yields 7 faults on that string with 3 frames.
Optimal farthest future yields 5 ideal lower bound.
example.answer: FIFO 7, LRU 6, Optimal 5 — Optimal best ideal, LRU better than FIFO, only FIFO can show Belady
